prompt: Write a short blog post about a small mishap around the house. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
# The Great Sourdough Flood

Last Saturday I decided I was finally going to become a Person Who Bakes Bread. I had a jar of sourdough starter, a brand-new Dutch oven, and a podcast promising that "anyone can do this."

Anyone, it turns out, does not include me before coffee.

The starter had been living on the counter for two weeks, happily bubbling away. Our friend Dana had gifted it to me with a handwritten label that read "Gerald." I took this as a sign that Gerald was low-maintenance. Gerald was not.

The recipe said to feed the starter, wait until it doubled, then mix the dough. I fed Gerald and went to fold laundry, fully intending to return in an hour. Instead I got sucked into sorting a drawer of mismatched socks, which is a rabbit hole with no bottom.

When I wandered back into the kitchen, I found that Gerald had doubled. And tripled. And then, apparently, decided that the jar was merely a suggestion. A pale, glossy ribbon of starter was creeping over the lip, down the side of the jar, across the counter, and toward the edge with the slow confidence of a horror movie blob.

I grabbed a dish towel and lunged. This was my second mistake. The first was the socks. The towel caught the jar's base, the jar tipped, and about a cup of living, bubbling, extremely sticky starter slid off the counter and landed directly on the open cabinet door below, then into my slippers.

If you have never had warm, yeasty goo seep into your socks, I can't recommend it. It feels the way a hug from a wet sponge would feel.

My partner wandered in, took in the scene, and asked, very gently, "Is this... the bread?" I said it was the *beginning* of the bread. They nodded the way you nod at someone standing on a ledge.

Cleanup took forty minutes. Starter, I learned, dries like cement and dissolves like regret. I scraped it off the cabinet with a spatula, then a butter knife, then, in a low moment, a fingernail.

Here's the strange part, though: I salvaged about half of Gerald and gave him a bigger jar. The next morning, I tried again, with coffee this time, and no socks. Three hours later I pulled out a loaf that was lopsided, a little dense, and absolutely delicious.

We ate half of it standing at the counter, still warm, smeared with butter.

Gerald now lives in a jar roughly the size of a flower vase. I check on him often. We have an understanding.

And my slippers? Still in the wash. Some wounds take time.
